fields.title: A Hidden Fire
fields.subtitle: The One Thing He Wanted to Know
fields.description: Simeon Nsibambi (1897–1978) was a Kampala health officer who had everything his society valued and could not stop being hungry for God. In September 1929 he asked a tired English missionary one question — what is missing, in me and in the church? — and the two days of Bible and prayer that followed are widely counted the spark of the East African Revival. He resigned his post, was thought mad for asking strangers about their souls, and then spent his last thirty-seven years too ill to leave his house while the movement he lit ran across five countries without him. Seven readings that tell his life in order and turn each stage of it on the reader, staying close to the little the record actually holds and saying so where it falls silent.

fields.title: A Man Who Had Arrived
fields.body_html:
A kingdom that had just changed its religion

To understand Simeon Nsibambi you have to understand how new his church was.

The first Christian missionaries reached the kingdom of Buganda in 1877, twenty years before he was born. Within a decade the new faith had gone deep enough into the young men of the royal court that the kabaka moved against it, and in 1886 a group of them were burned at Namugongo rather than give it up. Buganda then did something almost without parallel in Africa: it took up Christianity at speed, from the top down and the bottom up at once, until within a generation the church was not a foreign mission station but a national institution with Baganda clergy, Baganda chiefs in its pews, and a cathedral on Namirembe Hill.

Nsibambi was born into the generation after all of that, in 1897. He never knew the persecution. He inherited the settlement.

The man himself

By his early thirties he was a public health officer in Kampala — a sanitation man, responsible for the ordinary, unglamorous business of keeping a growing city from killing its own people through its water and its waste. He married Eva Bakaluba, and they would eventually have twelve children. He was a Muganda of standing, and a baptised, believing member of the Anglican Church of Uganda.

His father was Walusimbi Kimanje, a chief. He was schooled at Mengo High School and at King’s College, Budo, the training ground of Buganda’s leadership. In the First World War he served in the African Native Medical Corps and was decorated for distinguished service, and in 1920 — at about twenty-three — he was made Chief Health Officer in the Buganda king’s government. He was an athlete, a footballer and a wrestler, and a singer. He became a Christian in 1922, and married Eva Bakaluba about three years after that.

So the outward facts are not thin at all, and that is exactly the difficulty. By 1929 this was a man of thirty-two with a war record, a decoration, an education, a senior government post, a family and a faith. There is no gap in that life for God to fill. And the one thing no account disputes is that he was not satisfied.

At the height of his respectability, Simeon Nsibambi was not satisfied.

He looked at the church he had inherited — correct, established, second-generation — and at himself inside it, and concluded that something was missing from both. Weigh what it cost him to admit that. He was not a young man casting about for a direction. He was established. He held the thing that everyone around him agreed was worth holding.

The particular danger of a good position

There is a hunger that poverty produces and a hunger it cannot. The man who has nothing knows exactly what he lacks, and so does everyone who looks at him. The man who has everything and is still hungry is in a stranger position. He has no vocabulary for his own want. When he says he is dissatisfied, the people around him hear ingratitude, or ambition, or the restlessness of someone who does not know when he is well off.

So he learns not to say it. He becomes the most dangerous kind of respectable Christian: the one who has quietly agreed to stop expecting anything further. He is not a hypocrite. He believes what he professes. He simply no longer looks for it to make any difference he could name.

If you have been a Christian for a long time, you know this territory. You can tell when a sermon is sound. You know which songs you like. You could explain the gospel to a stranger without preparing. You have a place in the congregation and people would notice if you stopped coming. And somewhere underneath all of it, in a room you do not often open, there is a question you have stopped asking because asking it seemed ungrateful: is this all there is of God?

Discontent that is not sin

We are right to be suspicious of discontent. Most of it is appetite wearing a religious coat — wanting a bigger platform, a warmer feeling, a church that suits us better. That kind of restlessness is worth resisting, and Scripture spends a good deal of time telling us so.

But there is another kind, and the whole Bible assumes it. Moses had seen more of God than any man alive and asked to see His glory. David had the throne and wrote that his soul thirsted as a dry land. Paul had been caught up to the third heaven and still wrote that he pressed on, that he had not attained. These were not men in decline. They were men at their height, saying plainly that they had not come to the end of God.

The test is not whether you are dissatisfied. The test is what you are dissatisfied with, and what you are asking for. A man who wants a better position is restless. A man who wants more of God, and knows he cannot manufacture it, has begun to pray.

Where this leaves you

We do not know what Nsibambi's inner life was like in those years. Nobody recorded it, and it would be an act of invention to describe it — to put thoughts in his head, or a scene in his house, or words in his mouth on some particular evening. He left almost nothing of his own in writing. What we have is the shape his life took afterwards, and the shape is unmistakable: this was a man who had arrived and did not think arriving was enough.

That is the whole of chapter one, and it is enough to be going on with. Before anything happened to him, he wanted something. Before the meeting on the hill, before the resignation, before the movement that historians would eventually trace back to him, there was a man with a good job and a settled faith who would not stop being hungry.

You cannot organise a revival. You cannot schedule one. But you can refuse to be satisfied, and that refusal is not nothing — it is the one part of this whole story that was in Nsibambi's power, and it is the part that is in yours.

So begin where he began. Not with a plan. With an admission: that you have more religion than you have God, and that you would like that to change.

A prayer

Father, I have inherited more than I have sought. Save me from a faith that is correct and cold, held because it was handed to me and never because I went after it. Give me the holy discontent that will not settle, and keep me from mistaking it for ingratitude. Amen.

fields.title: The Question He Could Not Put Down
fields.body_html:
The Englishman who came to Kampala to rest

In September 1929 a medical missionary named John Edward Church — Joe Church to everyone — came over the border into Uganda for a few days off.

He was twenty-nine or thirty, an English doctor of the Ruanda Mission, and he had spent the previous two years running the hospital at Gahini in eastern Rwanda through famine and disease. By his own account he had come to the end of his own resources: tired, discouraged, and short of the thing he was supposed to be dispensing. He was not on a preaching tour. He was staying with friends on Namirembe Hill, the ridge above Kampala where the Anglican cathedral stands, and he was there to recover.

Nsibambi found him there and asked him a question.

The one thing he wanted to know

The wording is remembered slightly differently depending on who is telling it, but the substance is always the same: there is something missing — in me, and in the church of Uganda. Can you tell me what it is?

That question is the reason this book exists. Almost everything else about Nsibambi is disputed, thin, or reconstructed. This is not. It is the most solidly attested thing he ever said, and everything that follows in his life turns on it.

Church, as it happened, had something to say. He had absorbed the “victorious life” teaching of the Keswick conventions in England — a strand of holiness preaching concerned less with forgiveness than with the fullness of the Holy Spirit and a Christian life lived in power rather than defeat. It was not a subject he had mastered. It was a subject he was himself hungry about, which is probably why the conversation went where it did instead of ending politely.

Notice what he did not ask

He did not ask for a method. He did not ask what programme the mission was running, or what he might organise in his parish, or how to grow the church at Namirembe. He did not ask for a technique he could take away and apply.

He also did not ask for a diagnosis of somebody else. This is worth sitting with, because it is the rarer half. He said: there is something missing in me, and in the church. He named himself first. A man in his position could very easily have asked what was wrong with the younger generation, or the chiefs, or the missionaries, or the nominal Christians filling the pews. Instead he put himself at the front of the sentence.

And he asked it of a stranger. A tired one, at that — not a famous preacher, not a bishop, not anyone whose answer would have carried weight in Kampala. Nsibambi was a man of some standing asking a wrung-out doctor on holiday to tell him what was wrong with him. There is no way to do that while protecting your dignity. He evidently decided his dignity was the cheaper thing.

The question we ask instead

Most of us do ask questions about our faith. They are usually a slightly different shape.

We ask what should I do? — which is a good question, and also a safe one, because the answer arrives as a task and a task can be completed. We ask why is the church like this? — which locates the trouble at a comfortable distance. We ask how do I feel more? — which turns out to be a question about ourselves wearing the clothes of a question about God.

Nsibambi's question is harder than all three because it is unguarded. It admits a lack without knowing the remedy. It hands the diagnosis to somebody else. It leaves him standing there with nothing to offer and no idea what will be said next.

That is why the question is rare, and it is why it works. You cannot ask it and remain in control of the outcome.

Asking it out loud

There is a difference between privately suspecting you are missing something and saying so to another person. The first costs nothing. It can go on for decades, and often does; a quiet ache that never becomes a sentence.

The second changes things, and not only because the other person might have an answer. It changes things because saying it out loud is the moment you stop managing the problem. As long as the hunger stays inside you, you can decide what it means, when to attend to it, how seriously to take it. Spoken, it is out of your hands.

Nsibambi had presumably been hungry for years. We do not know; nobody wrote it down. What we know is that in September 1929 he stopped keeping it to himself, and that within the decade a movement was running across East Africa that historians would trace to that conversation.

Not because the question was magic. Because a question like that is a door, and he opened it.

Your turn

Is there a person you could ask? Not an audience — one person, who knows God better than you do, or differently, or longer. Someone whose answer might cost you something to hear.

And could you frame it as he did: not what should I do, not why is everyone else like this, but what is missing in me?

You may not get an answer worth having. Joe Church was, by his own reckoning, in no condition to be anybody's teacher that week. He gave what he had anyway. That is usually how this goes.

Ask anyway. The value is not only in the reply.

A prayer

Lord, I have grown skilled at asking questions that keep me safe. Teach me to ask the one that does not: what is missing in me? Give me the humility to put it to someone who may answer plainly, and the courage to still be standing there when they do. Amen.

fields.title: Two Tired Men and an Open Bible
fields.body_html:
What happened on the hill

The two men did not let the conversation end that day. Over what the accounts remember as roughly two days they sat together on Namirembe Hill with the Bible open between them, working through what Scripture says about the filling of the Holy Spirit, and praying.

They prayed to put away every sin they knew of. They prayed to be filled. They prayed to hold nothing back. That is the entire event: two men, a book, a couple of days, and prayer.

Church went back to Gahini a changed man — those who tell the story say he returned in the power of Pentecost — and what he carried back began to work through the mission there. The deeper change was in Nsibambi, and he did not go quietly back to his old life.

Historians of the East African Revival generally point to that weekend as the spark. Within a few years an awakening was moving through Uganda and Rwanda, and eventually through Kenya, Tanzania and Burundi, that would run for most of the twentieth century and touch millions of people. Its people were called the balokole — the saved ones — and the Luganda hymn they sang, Tukutendereza Yesu, we praise You, Jesus, became the sound of the whole movement.

It began with two discouraged men who could not let a conversation go.

The scale is the point

We are so accustomed to thinking of spiritual movements as things that are launched that it is worth stopping on how completely this was not.

There was no venue. There was no invitation, no advertising, no committee, no funding, no name for what they were doing. Neither man had a strategy. One of them was on holiday because he was exhausted. Neither had any way of knowing that anyone would ever hear about it. If nothing had come of it, nothing would have been lost, because nothing had been staked.

And this is exactly the sort of thing that we, who like to be useful, find almost impossible to value. Two days of reading and praying with one other person produces nothing you can show anyone. There is no report to file at the end of it. In the economy most of us actually live by — where a day counts if something was accomplished — that weekend was a write-off.

What they actually did

Strip the story of its outcome and look at the practice, because the practice is imitable and the outcome is not.

They read Scripture together, slowly, over an extended stretch of time. Not a passage before a meeting. Days.

They talked about one thing. They did not range across every question either of them had. They stayed on the fullness of the Spirit until they were done with it, or it was done with them.

They prayed about their own sin by name. Both of them. The senior missionary and the Ugandan layman brought their own failures into it, rather than one man counselling the other.

They refused to stop early. The detail that keeps recurring in the accounts is that they could not leave it alone — that it took the better part of two days, that the conversation would not release them.

Every one of those four is available to you this month. None of them requires permission, funding, gifting, or a platform. What they require is time you have not currently set aside and a companion honest enough to be uncomfortable with.

Why two, and not one

Nsibambi could have prayed alone. He had presumably been doing exactly that for years. Something about this was different, and the difference was that another person was in the room.

There is a kind of honesty that only becomes possible in front of a witness. Alone, we confess in general terms, because in general terms it is less painful and there is nobody to notice the vagueness. Alone, we decide when we have prayed enough. Alone, we can be very devout and change nothing, and nobody will ever know.

Two people praying about their real sin is a different act. It has a cost the private version does not, and the cost is most of the point. The movement that came out of that weekend built its whole culture on this: walking in the light, they called it, meaning open honesty before God and one another, out loud, in company.

They did not invent that idea in a seminar. They discovered it on a hill in Kampala because there happened to be two of them.

The uncomfortable arithmetic

If the East African Revival can be traced to two men praying for two days, then the smallness of what you can do is not the obstacle you have been treating it as.

That cuts both ways, and the second way is the sharper. It means the reason you have not seen more is probably not that you lack scale, resources, or gifting. Those were absent here too. It is more likely that you have never actually cleared two days, never asked anyone to sit with you, and never stayed on one thing long enough for it to cost you anything.

God did not need Namirembe to be a large meeting. He needed it to be an honest one.

A prayer

Father, I have filled my calendar with things that can be reported and left no room for the thing that cannot. Give me two days, and someone honest to spend them with, and the stubbornness not to get up early. Fill me, and do not let me settle for having asked. Amen.

fields.title: The Cost He Counted
fields.body_html:
He gave up the post

After Namirembe, Nsibambi resigned his public health job and gave himself to prayer and preaching. That much is agreed on by everyone who tells the story.

He did not do it alone, and he did not drift. He gathered others. A group formed around him in Kampala who were known as the Abaka — the men of fire — men who had come into the same experience and would not keep quiet about it. Among them was his own younger brother, Blasio Kigozi, whom Nsibambi brought into a living faith and who would shortly go south to join Joe Church at Gahini. What had been one man's private hunger was becoming a company.

What nobody records is the part we would most like to know. We do not know how long he thought about resigning, whether Eva agreed, what it did to the household, whether anyone talked him out of it and failed, or whether he ever regretted it. He and Eva had a large family — twelve children in the end, among them a son, Apolo, who would one day be Prime Minister of Uganda. A man with that many mouths to feed does not walk away from a government salary absent-mindedly.

So we have the decision without the deliberation. We know what he did and not what it cost him, which is the reverse of how we normally hear such stories, and probably healthier.

Against the version you have heard before

The way this kind of story usually gets told, the sacrifice is presented as easy — the man was so full of joy that the salary simply stopped mattering. That telling is popular because it is comfortable. It removes the cost by removing the weight of what was given up.

There is no evidence for it here, and some reason to doubt it. His neighbours evidently thought he had lost his mind, which is not the reaction people have to a decision that looks obviously sensible. Whatever the inside of it was like, from the outside it looked like a respectable man throwing away the thing he had spent his life acquiring.

Do not let anyone sell you the frictionless version. If following God has never cost you anything you actually wanted, you may not yet have been asked. When you are, it will feel like a loss, because it will be one.

What he was not doing

It is worth being careful here, because this chapter could easily become a sermon telling you to quit your job, and that would be a misreading.

Nsibambi did not resign because employment is unspiritual. He had held that post for years as a believing man, and the work itself — keeping a city's water and waste from killing its people — is about as plain a piece of loving your neighbour as a job can be. Nothing suggests he came to think it was beneath him.

He resigned because he had been given something he could not hold and also hold on to everything else. That is a different thing from despising ordinary work. Most people who have been genuinely changed by God stay exactly where they are and are different there. Some do not. The question is not which category is holier. The question is whether there is anything you have decided in advance that God may not ask for.

The thing that is actually being asked

Because that is the transferable part. Almost none of us will be asked to resign a post. All of us have a list.

The list is usually unspoken and quite short, and you can find it by noticing where you go quiet when you pray. There is the plan you have made for the next ten years. There is the standard of living you have come to regard as the floor rather than the ceiling. There is the relationship you would keep even if you were shown it was doing you harm. There is the reputation you have built and would find it very hard to be thought a fool in front of.

You do not have to give any of those away this afternoon. But you might ask yourself honestly whether you have put them outside the negotiation — whether, in the quiet arithmetic you actually run your life by, they are simply not on the table.

Because the decision Nsibambi made was not really made on the day he resigned. It was made earlier, when he stopped keeping a list of exceptions. The resignation was just where it became visible.

Counted, not swept aside

Jesus told people to sit down and work out the cost before building the tower, which is a strange thing for Him to say if the cost were nothing. He assumed it would be real and expected them to look at it squarely first.

So do that. Not with the pretence that it will not hurt. Count it. Name the thing. Ask whether you believe that what God gives is worth more than what He asks for — not in the abstract, where everyone says yes, but in the specific case, with the actual figure in front of you.

Nsibambi seems to have concluded that it was. He was not, by any account, a reckless man. He was a sanitation officer; his whole professional life had been careful. He counted, and then he went.

A prayer

Lord, I keep a quiet list of things I have decided You may not ask for. You know every item on it better than I do. I am not brave enough to hand it over all at once, so begin with one: show me which, and make me willing before I am asked. Amen.

fields.title: “Are You Saved?”
fields.body_html:
The question he asked everybody

After his resignation, Nsibambi became known for one habit above all others. He stopped people — on the road, in the market, at the gate — and asked them whether they were saved.

Not everyone was delighted. The best-remembered reaction is from an exasperated missionary who complained to Joe Church about what his friend had started: he has gone mad, and is going round everywhere asking people if they are saved. He has just left my gardener.

That sentence has survived for nearly a century because it is funny, and because the person who said it was so completely wrong.

Meanwhile the thing was spreading beyond him. Blasio Kigozi, the brother he had led to faith, was ordained deacon and sent to Gahini, and became a burning evangelist in his own right — praying for the mission, preaching for conviction, pressing the same question Nsibambi pressed on strangers in Kampala. In January 1936 Kigozi was called back to Uganda to put the case for revival before the church's synod in Kampala. He delivered his message. He had contracted tick fever on the journey, and within days he was dead, still in his twenties.

It was Nsibambi who buried him. The funeral was on Cathedral Hill at Namirembe, crowded, and the older brother officiated at the grave of the younger. The word Blasio had carried to the synod was cut into his headstone.

And the young man’s death, coming straight after the plea, did more to press the case for revival on the Ugandan church than the plea alone had done. The movement went on growing, and it grew through a grave that Simeon Nsibambi stood beside.

The offence in it

It is worth being honest about why this makes us wince, because it does, and pretending otherwise gets us nowhere.

Asking a stranger about his soul breaks a rule that almost every society agrees on: that a person's inner life is his own business unless he offers it. To ask is to presume — to suggest that you know something about his condition that he has not told you, and that it is urgent enough to override the ordinary courtesy between strangers.

And the complaint about the gardener has a further sting in it. It was a complaint about class. The missionary was not objecting that Nsibambi had spoken to a person; he was objecting that Nsibambi had gone through his household and spoken to the help. The revival that came out of all this would spend the next fifty years breaking down exactly those walls — between tribes, between races, between the respectable and everyone else. It started with a man who did not observe them.

What it assumes

Strip away the awkwardness and look at the belief underneath, because the habit is only as good as the conviction driving it.

To ask a stranger whether he is saved, you must think three things are true at once. That the question has an answer. That the answer matters more than the awkwardness of asking. And that this person — a gardener, a trader, someone you will never see again — is worth the cost of the awkwardness to you.

Most of us assent to all three and behave as though we assented to none. We would say the question matters eternally, and then decline to ask it because the moment was not right, or the relationship was not deep enough, or it would have seemed pushy. We have found a way to hold the belief without the belief costing us anything at all.

Nsibambi's neighbours thought he had gone mad. What they were actually observing was a man whose behaviour had caught up with his convictions. That is unusual enough to look like insanity.

Not a licence

This does not mean the criticism was baseless in every case, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise.

There is a way of asking that is really about the asker — that treats a person as an item to be processed, that presses for a form of words, that mistakes having said something for having loved somebody. The question can be a weapon. It can be used to embarrass, to establish superiority, to discharge an obligation so you can stop thinking about the person.

What made Nsibambi's version different is not recorded in any transcript, but it is legible in the outcome. People kept coming to him. For decades afterwards, when he could no longer go out at all, they came to his house. Nobody seeks out a man who once made them feel small. They sought him out because whatever was in the question, it was not contempt.

The smaller version you can actually do

You will probably not start stopping strangers in the street, and this chapter is not going to tell you that you must.

But there is a smaller version, and it is harder to dodge. There are people you already know — at work, in your family, on your street — with whom you have had a hundred conversations and never once raised the only subject you say is ultimate. Not because the moment never came. Because you decided, each time, that it was not worth the discomfort.

Start there. One person. Not a technique, not a script, not an ambush: just a real question, asked because you actually want to know the answer, from someone who has made himself safe enough to ask it.

And be prepared to be thought strange. Nsibambi was. The judgement of his neighbours was that he had gone mad; the judgement of history is that he was a father of a movement. Both were looking at the same man doing the same thing.

A prayer

Father, I have had a hundred conversations with people I say I love and never once raised the only subject I call ultimate. Forgive the cowardice I have been calling tact. Give me one person this week, and the plain words to ask, and a heart in it that is not contempt. Amen.

fields.title: When the Strength Goes
fields.body_html:
Thirty-seven years indoors

In 1941 Nsibambi's health broke. Joe Church, who knew him well, described the illness only as a weakness; no better diagnosis has come down to us. From then until his death in 1978 he lived largely confined to his home near Namirembe Cathedral, an invalid.

Do the arithmetic, because it is easy to read past. He was about forty-four when he fell ill. He was eighty-one when he died. The man remembered as a father of the East African Revival spent roughly thirty-seven years — the larger part of his adult life, by a wide margin — unable to do the thing he had given up everything to do.

He did not stop the street preaching because he had finished. He stopped because his body would not carry him out of the house.

What was happening outside the house

And the movement did not pause for him.

Through the 1940s and 1950s the revival ran on through the Anglican and Protestant churches of Uganda, Rwanda, Kenya, Tanzania and Burundi. Its marks were the ones set on that hillside: repentance, confession of sin out loud, what the balokole called walking in the light — open honesty before God and before each other — and the singing of Tukutendereza Yesu wherever they gathered. It cut across tribe and across the line between missionary and African, which in colonial East Africa was not a small thing to cut across.

It produced people. Erica Sabiti, who would become the first African archbishop of Uganda. Festo Kivengere, the evangelist who would preach alongside Billy Graham and who, after Idi Amin murdered his archbishop, wrote a book called I Love Idi Amin. And Janani Luwum himself, killed in 1977 for standing up to that regime.

Nsibambi was in a room the whole time, on his knees, receiving whoever climbed the hill to see him. He outlived Luwum by a year.

Refusing the tidy version

There is a way of telling this that makes it comfortable, and it is worth naming so that we can decline it. The comfortable version says: God withdrew him from public work so that he could pray, and prayer was the greater ministry, so nothing was lost.

The second half of that is true. The first half is a guess, and the last clause is not true at all.

Something was lost. A man who loved to stop people on the road could not go out to the road. A man whose great gift was face-to-face with strangers was reduced to whoever could climb the hill to see him. We should not smooth that over. The Bible does not; it is full of people who wanted to do more than they were permitted to do, and it does not always explain why.

What we can say is what he did with it, and that is the only part of this that is ours to imitate anyway.

What he did with it

He prayed, and he received whoever came.

That is a short sentence for thirty-seven years, and it is worth holding it next to the paragraphs above. Everything in them — the five countries, the archbishops, the hymn going up in churches he would never see — was happening to a movement whose root was a man in a room, on his knees, watching almost none of it.

Whether he heard of Luwum's murder, and what he prayed when he did, nobody wrote down. It is exactly the kind of detail that would make this chapter more moving, and exactly the kind we are not entitled to invent.

For anyone whose strength has gone

You may be reading this from inside a version of the same thing. Illness that did not lift. Age that took the work away. A season of caring for someone else that has swallowed everything you used to be able to give. Something has closed, and you are still here, and the arithmetic of your usefulness looks bad to you.

Two things are worth saying, and the order matters.

The first is that your grief about it is not unbelief. Nowhere does Scripture require you to pretend the loss is not a loss. Paul asked three times for the thorn to be removed; the asking was not held against him. Whatever peace is available here is not the peace of deciding you never wanted the other thing.

The second is that the room is not a waiting area. This is the part the tidy version gets right even though it arrives there too cheaply. Nsibambi's thirty-seven years were not the epilogue to his ministry. On the evidence, they were most of it — longer than the street preaching, longer than the health office, longer than everything before them put together.

The parable in it

There is something fitting in how it turned out, and it is not a coincidence anyone arranged.

The movement Nsibambi lit was never really about platforms. Its convictions were repentance, confession, walking in the light, and prayer — none of which need a crowd, and all of which can be done by a man in a single room. That its father should spend his last decades unseen, doing precisely those four things, is not an irony. It is the movement's own message, demonstrated by the one person best placed to demonstrate it.

He had already given it the only thing that mattered: a hunger for holiness and a habit of prayer. He went on giving both from a place where nobody could see him do it.

If you are in such a place, you are not out of the story. You may be nearer the centre of it than the people outside who are visibly busy.

A prayer

Lord, when my strength goes, do not let me believe I have gone with it. Teach me that a closed door is not an ending, and let me grieve honestly without concluding that You have finished with me. Make the small room a place of intercession. Amen.

fields.title: What a Small Room Can Hold
fields.body_html:
He wrote nothing

Simeon Nsibambi died in 1978, an old man, in the house he had barely left for thirty-seven years.

He left no books. No famous sermons, no collected letters, no journal that has come down to us. Almost every sentence attributed to him in this book reaches us second-hand, through people who heard him or wrote about him afterwards. Even the question that changed his life — there is something missing in me and in the church, can you tell me what it is — survives in slightly different words depending on who is telling it.

By almost any measure we normally use, that is a thin record. And yet the movement that came out of that hillside weekend ran for the better part of a century across five countries and has not stopped.

What actually survived

It is worth being precise about what carried, because it was not the things we usually try to build.

Not an organisation. Nsibambi did not run the revival; there is no institution he founded that we can point to as his. Not a body of teaching — he wrote none. Not a method, not a brand, not a network he presided over. He resigned his only formal position and then, for most of the remaining decades, could not leave his house.

What survived was a set of habits in other people. Confess your sin out loud. Walk in the light with each other. Ask people about their souls. Expect God to fill you and do not settle for less. Those things spread person to person, which is a slow and unimpressive method, and also the only one that does not decay when the founder stops attending.

Kivengere had it. Luwum had it, and it cost him his life. Neither of them learned it from a book of Nsibambi's, because there wasn't one.

The uncomfortable comparison

Set that against what most of us are quietly hoping to leave behind, and the contrast is not flattering.

We would like to be remembered. We would like there to be something with our name on it — a work, a role, a reputation, a body of output that proves the years were not wasted. This is not a wicked desire, but it is a fragile one, and Nsibambi's life is a fairly direct challenge to it. He has no output. He has descendants in the faith.

And notice that he could not have engineered this if he had tried. Everything that made him influential was, from his point of view, either a loss or an embarrassment: he gave up his position, he was thought insane by his neighbours, and then he was taken out of circulation entirely by an illness nobody could even name. If he had been asked at any point to describe his strategy, he would have had nothing to say.

What this asks of you

Not that you resign anything. Not that you seek obscurity, which is its own kind of vanity if you seek it.

Only this: that you stop measuring your life by what will be visible afterwards, and start measuring it by what is true of you now. Are you hungry? Are you honest with someone? Do you pray when nobody is counting? Is there any person who is different because of what you have said to them about God?

Those questions have nothing to do with scale, and they are the only ones this story rewards. A man asked them of himself in 1929 with no idea what would follow, and the honest truth is that he never really saw what followed — he was indoors for most of it.

A hidden fire

The image the whole story keeps returning to is fire, and it is worth taking the metaphor seriously for a moment, because fire is a poor illustration of everything we usually mean by influence.

Fire does not spread by planning. It spreads by contact. It does not need the first flame to remain lit in order to keep going; it needs something next to it that will catch. A fire that has spread does not remember which spark began it, and does not need to.

Nsibambi's flame was lit on a hill in Kampala over two days, and for the last half of his life it was hidden inside a house where hardly anyone saw it burning. It went on being fire the whole time.

Whatever God does with your life, He is unlikely to consult you about the shape of it. He did not consult Nsibambi. What was asked of him was the same thing that is asked of you: be genuinely hungry, be honest with somebody, hold nothing back, and keep praying when the visible part of your usefulness has been taken away.

That is the whole of it. It is not a strategy. It has never needed to be.

A prayer

Father, I want to be remembered, and I am not sure that is a holy wish. Take it, and give me instead what You gave him: a real hunger, an honest friend, nothing held back, and the willingness to burn where nobody is watching. Let something outlive me that does not have my name on it. Amen.

No famous sermons, no collected letters, no journal that has come down to us. Almost every sentence attributed to him in this book reaches us second-hand, through people who heard him or wrote about him afterwards. Even the question that changed his life — there is something missing in me and in the church, can you tell me what it is — survives in slightly different words depending on who is telling it. By almost any measure we normally use, that is a thin record. And yet the movement that came out of that hillside weekend ran for the better part of a century across five countries and has not stopped. What actually survived It is worth being precise about what carried, because it was not the things we usually try to build. Not an organisation. Nsibambi did not run the revival; there is no institution he founded that we can point to as his. Not a body of teaching — he wrote none. Not a method, not a brand, not a network he presided over. Walk in the light with each other. Ask people about their souls. Expect God to fill you and do not settle for less.
